html:
Mongkut was King of Siam from 1851 to 1868, the fourth king of the Chakri dynasty, known as Rama IV. He opened his country to Western trade and ideas on his own terms, helping Siam stay independent while its neighbours fell to Britain and France.

Passed over for the throne in 1824, he spent 27 years as a Buddhist monk. He studied the Pali scriptures and founded a stricter reform movement that became the Dhammayuttika order. He also learned Latin, English and Western astronomy from missionaries. In 1833, on a pilgrimage to Sukhothai, he found the stone inscription later attributed to Ramkhamhaeng.

As king, he chose to bend rather than break. In 1855 he signed the Bowring Treaty with Britain, which fixed low tariffs, ended royal trade monopolies and gave British subjects their own courts. Similar treaties with other powers followed. Rice exports boomed. He hired foreign advisers and teachers, among them Anna Leonowens, whose much embellished memoir later inspired The King and I.

He calculated in advance the total solar eclipse of August 1868 and went south to watch it with foreign guests. He caught malaria on the trip and died weeks later. His son Chulalongkorn carried his reforms much further.
